record.original_question: Find a proof of the four-colour theorem that does not rely on computer verification.

evidence.quote: Problem 5.1 Find a non-computer proof of the four-colour theorem.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
The four-colour theorem states: for every finite loopless planar graph $G$, there exists a proper vertex colouring $c: V(G) \to \{1,2,3,4\}$ such that $c(u) \neq c(v)$ whenever $uv \in E(G)$. Equivalently, the regions of any planar map can be coloured with at most four colours so that any two regions sharing a boundary arc receive different colours.

All known proofs of this theorem reduce the problem to checking a large but finite set of "reducible configurations" forming an "unavoidable set", and this case analysis has only been carried out with the aid of computer verification (originating with the 1976 proof and refined in later proofs).

Problem: Produce a proof of the four-colour theorem that does not rely on computer verification, i.e., a proof whose every step can be checked by hand by a human mathematician in a reasonable amount of time.
artifact.status_search_result: No human-checkable proof of the four-colour theorem is known as of 2026. All accepted proofs (Appel–Haken 1976; Robertson–Sanders–Seymour–Thomas 1997; Gonthier's 2005 Coq formalization) rely on computer verification of a large set of reducible configurations. Finding a non-computer proof remains a widely cited open problem.

status_evidence.title: Four color theorem - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: The four color theorem was the first major theorem to be proved using a computer... To date, no proof of the four color theorem has been found that does not require a computer.
